analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to handle care approvals electronically, publicly report denials, and respond faster.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2025 with 70 cosponsors from both parties — more than two-thirds of the Senate — and was referred to the Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans are private insurance plans that cover the majority of Medicare beneficiaries, and they can refuse to cover a scan, procedure, or drug until a doctor gets plan approval first — a process called prior authorization. This bill would require those plans to run that process through a standardized electronic system instead of fax machines and portals, publicly report each year how many requests they approve, deny, and overturn on appeal (and how long decisions take), let patients and doctors see the criteria plans use to say no, and let the government set deadlines for how fast plans must answer.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans who have care delayed or denied while waiting for plan approval, plus the doctors and hospitals that lose time and money fighting those denials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans would have to establish an electronic prior authorization program with secure, standardized electronic transmission of requests, responses, and documentation — faxes, basic electronic forms, and proprietary portals that don't meet federal standards wouldn't count.

Plans would have to report annually to the government — which would publish it on a public CMS website — a detailed list per plan of what services they subject to prior authorization, the percentage and number of requests approved and denied, how many denials were appealed and how many appeals succeeded, the average and median hours to decide each type of request, and how often they used artificial intelligence or automated tools to make decisions.

Enrollees, on request, and their doctors would gain access to the criteria a plan uses to decide prior authorization requests, and plans would have to consult enrollees and providers, consider waiving prior authorization for high-performing providers, and review annually which services actually need it.

The Health and Human Services Secretary could set binding timeframes — such as 24 hours — for plans to answer prior authorization requests, including for expedited and real-time decisions on routinely approved services.

The bill directs CMS and health IT officials to report by January 1, 2028 on the feasibility of real-time approvals for routinely approved items and to analyze how artificial-intelligence-driven denials affect patient access, including for rural and low-income beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who would face compliance costs building electronic systems and reporting data, and would lose the informational advantage that lets them deny care without public scrutiny — costs that could be passed into premiums or reduced benefits.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not limit when plans may deny care or require a doctor rather than an algorithm to make the final call — it makes denials visible and faster to process, but a plan could still deny the same services afterward.

The response-time deadlines are permissive: the Secretary 'may establish' timeframes rather than being required to impose a specific clock, leaving the strength of the timeliness guarantee to future regulation.
Compliance costs for insurers could be passed to beneficiaries through higher premiums or lower supplemental benefits, and providers face a transition to new electronic systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and immediate for the more than half of Medicare beneficiaries in Medicare Advantage plans whose care waits on plan approval: faster answers, public data on denial rates, and access to the rules plans apply. The costs are administrative — building electronic systems and reporting data — which is modest relative to the delay and denial burden the bill targets. The main weakness is that the bill reforms the process, not the substance: plans keep the power to deny, and the enforcement teeth depend on future regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2025, and the committee has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since then; with the 119th Congress still in session, it sits waiting.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, with a list of original cosponsors including Sens. Mark Warner, Maggie Hassan, John Fetterman, Bill Cassidy, and Josh Hawley — a notably bipartisan launch.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, and the complete action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the present.
The bill gathered 70 cosponsors, split 37 Democrats, 32 Republicans, and 1 Independent — roughly 70% of the Senate.
This is a reintroduction of a proposal that has been offered in several Congresses; an earlier version passed the House unanimously in 2022 but never received a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off so far: the bill has sat in the Finance Committee with no hearing or vote, so plans continue operating under the current prior authorization rules with no public denial reporting, no electronic mandate, and no binding response deadlines.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan original cosponsor list spanning both parties, including Sens. Warner, Hassan, Fetterman, Cassidy, and Hawley.

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner and the other 69 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill support from about 70% of the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Mike Crapo)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 20, 2025 and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the months since.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Industry whose plans the bill would regulate
against.what_they_did: Prior versions of this bill drew opposition from Medicare Advantage insurers and their trade association, who argue prior authorization controls costs and the mandates add compliance burden; no industry stance specific to this 2025 bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The 70 cosponsors split 37 Democrats, 32 Republicans, and 1 Independent, and the original sponsor list pairs Republicans like Marshall, Cassidy, and Hawley with Democrats like Warner, Fetterman, and Klobuchar — the bill's blocker is not partisan opposition but inaction in committee.

industries.note: Plans profit in part because prior authorization delays and denials reduce spending on care, and the industry has opposed prior versions of this bill. The bill makes their denial practices public at the plan level and speeds up responses, which removes the informational advantage they currently hold.

Providers spend significant staff time chasing approvals by fax and portal and appealing denials; standardized electronic submission and published criteria would cut that administrative burden and get patients treated sooner.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic records vendors
industries.note: The electronic prior authorization mandate creates a market for standardized electronic transaction systems, which vendors of medical software would build and sell to plans and providers.

analysis.trajectory: History points one way: an earlier version passed the House unanimously in 2022 and still died in the Senate. With 70 cosponsors this bill has the votes to pass if it reached the floor, but Medicare Advantage legislation typically moves only when attached to a larger health package — so unless leadership folds it into a year-end or Medicare-related bill, it will likely sit in the Finance Committee until the 119th Congress ends.
